L115: Foreword
L116: ## I am a mathematician. Mathematics have filled my life; a passion for research
L117: and teaching, as a professor both in the university and at the Ecole Polytech­
L118: nique. I have thought about the role of mathematics, research, and teaching,
L119: in my life in and the lives of others; I have pondered on the mental processes
L120: of research, and for decades I have devoted myself to urgently necessary re­
L121: forms within the university and the Ecole Polytechnique. Some of my reflections
L122: are contained in this book, as well as a description of the course of my life.
L123: However, I do not discuss the university reforms, since I have written many
L124: articles and books on the subject. Inevitably, mathematics appear in this book;
L125: one cannot conceive of an autobiography of a mathematician which contains no
L126: mathematics. I have written about them in a historical form which should be
L127: accessible to large non-specialist sections of the scientific public; readers im­
L128: pervious to their charm may simply skip them. They concern only about fifteen
L129: per cent of the volume.
L130: I have been involved in many activities besides mathematics, sometimes to
L131: such a point that my research suffered. I devoted a large part of my time to
L132: struggling for the oppressed, for human rights and the rights of peoples, first as
L133: a Trotskyist, and later outside of any party. It was normal that I would wish to
L134: describe these activities, so they will be remembered in the future. Furthermore,
L135: I have had another great passion, almost as intense as that for mathematics,
L136: but which I did not describe here at great length: entomology, and particularly
L137: butterfly collecting, but more generally the whole field of biology. It would have
L138: been too long to speak of that here, except for some anecdotes; I hope some
L139: day to write a book about my butterfly-hunting adventures during more than
L140: thirty trips to the tropics.
L141: There are many people I wish to thank for their help. I showed several
L142: chapters to various colleagues, and to my wife and daughter; their advice was
L143: very precious to me. I am grateful to Odile Jacob for having accepted, with
L144: typical enthusiasm and dynamism, to publish a book written by a mathematician.
L145: I thank Mireille de Maistre for taking care of my scientific administration, thus
L146: providing me with the time necessary to write. I took great pleasure in my truly
L147: viii A Mathematician Grappling with his Century
L148: agreeable three years’ collaboration with Isabelle Rozenbaumas. She read all
L149: the chapters with the competence of a translator, which enabled her to help me
L150: polish the style, without losing anything of my thought or my personality, so
L151: that everyone who knows me recognizes me in the book and feels, as certain
L152: readers have told me, that they can “hear the sound of my voice”.
L153: Introduction
L154: The Garden of Eden
L155: ## My mother always wanted a country house. As a little girl, she dreamed of
L156: being a shepherdess and adored nature, gardens, animals and flowers. When my
L157: parents bought the property of Autouillet, in September 1926 - “for a mouthful
L158: of bread”1), they always said -, they were already reasonably well-off: my
L159: father was a surgeon. I was just getting better from polio, which I had caught in
L160: July. It left few traces, but it did leave me physically weak for my whole life,
L161: not really able to walk a long way or to run and jump. I was eleven, and my
L162: brothers Daniel and Bertrand were nine and seven. My parents had searched
L163: for years, but they had missed a lot of opportunities because of my father’s
L164: professional conscience, which trembled for the life of his patients after each
L165: operation. In those days there were no antibiotics and postoperational infections
L166: were frequent.
L167: Les Closeaux (the closed waters) covered two and a half hectares and in­
L168: cluded an eleven-room house and a garden with two meadows at the end of
L169: it. My mother loved bric-a-brac and antiques. She decorated the interior with
L170: furniture, objets d’art and pictures, all of which disappeared after a number of
L171: robberies, doubtless committed with the cooperation of various antique dealers.
L172: Now we have installed an alarm system, which cost almost as much as whatever
L173: remained to steal.
L174: My mother went to antique fairs and made numerous acquisitions. The an­
L175: tique dealers knew her and would whisper: “Madame Schwartz, there’s nothing
L176: for you here. You know that we’re the ones who buy antiques, and you have
L177: to buy them from us. We’ll raise the auction prices as much as we have to to
L178: make sure you don’t get a thing.” But she was a real collector and ended up
L179: wearing them down with sheer persistence.
L180: In the living room there are two large paintings showing my father at around
L181: forty-five years old and my mother at twenty-five, just before my birth. I like
L182: the portrait of my father a lot; my mother’s is enchanting. It is just exactly as
L183: she was when I was a child. Every time we go to Autouillet and I enter the
L184: ## 1) A typical French expression meaning “for a song”
L185: 
L186: 2 A Mathematician Grappling with his Century
L187: living room, I look at her with emotion: she is so sweet, so beautiful. In spite of
L188: the alteration brought on by her many years (she died at the age of eighty-four),
L189: I never stopped seeing her as she looked in her flowering youth.
L190: The house is located at the entrance to the property. If, from there, you
L191: look towards the garden, it falls into several grand sections. To the left lies a
L192: greenhouse which we never kept up; it only has one pane now, but for a long
L193: time it was covered with a thick and very perfumed honeysuckle. Also to the
L194: left, a bit farther on, there is a vegetable garden of about 50 meters by 30,
L195: whose paths are edged by boxtrees probably over a hundred years old. The
L196: fruit trees are mainly apple and pear trees. At the bottom, you discover a little
L197: marvel: the outbuildings of an old eighteenth century castle, with precious tile
L198: rooves. The castle itself has disappeared, carried off stone by stone, apparently,
L199: by an American, and rebuilt somewhere in the US. But the outbuildings remain
L200: a splendid antique: we lodged the gardener Charles and his wife Alphonsine
L201: there.
L202: Beyond the greenhouse, a large lawn spreads more than fifty meters towards
L203: the outbuildings. It used to be covered by high grasses. It was a memorable
L204: delight for my brothers and me. I used to roll and wallow in the untamed
L205: grasses and admire all the beautiful flowers, particularly the big wild daisies.
L206: But they were soon replaced by a neat French garden. It was very charming
L207: though it didn’t correspond to my taste as much as the wild lawn. As children,
L208: we used to lie on our backs after dinner to watch for falling stars. A juniper bush
L209: which we planted at the bottom of the garden when I was young, and which
L210: was about two meters high back then, now measures a good twelve meters. It’s
